extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in journalism, media ethics, and the Pulitzer Prize
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and considerations for assessing whether an awarded piece or journalist should retain honors (here: debate over rescinding a Pulitzer for Walter Duranty). Focuses on evidence of deception, institutional responsibility, historical context, and precedents for revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulitzer revocation evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "clear and convincing evidence of deliberate deception"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pulitzer board in its 2003 review said it found no "clear and convincing evidence of deliberate deception" and therefore decided against withdrawing Duranty's award. This phrasing functions as the board's threshold for revoking a prize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent for revocation: confession/admission of fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: The board withdrew a prize in 1981 after a reporter confessed to fabricating her award-winning story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit admission of fabrication by a prize recipient has been treated as grounds for revocation; used as a concrete precedent distinguishing from disputed or contextual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award as an accolade for reporter performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A Pulitzer Prize implies an accolade for the reporter's performance, not just an isolated piece of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill Keller argues that if a reporter's overall performance was shameful, that undercuts the legitimacy of keeping the award. This criterion treats the recipient's broader integrity and body of work as relevant to retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional responsibility and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: By publishing discredited coverage, a paper can be said to have fallen short of its journalistic mission and should comprehensively detail its lapses to ensure they are not repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations are expected to acknowledge institutional failures, explain them publicly, and take remedial steps; this is part of assessing whether honors should remain attached to the institution or individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of threats, coercion, or external censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a journalist was censored, threatened, bribed or otherwise constrained when publishing questionable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes foreign correspondents were often censored and threatened; such mitigating circumstances may weigh against labeling reporting as deliberate deception and against revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and framing (euphemisms vs explicit naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of euphemisms (e.g., saying "malnutrition" instead of "famine") and other framing choices that downplay or obscure facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic and lexical choices that minimize severity can be evidence of problematic reporting or culpable obfuscation; assessing accuracy includes analyzing tone and terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding known facts from the public record
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to publish or to disclose knowledge of scale or severity (e.g., privately acknowledging deaths but not reporting them publicly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reporter had access to credible information about atrocities and did not disclose it, that omission is a substantive factor in judging the integrity of the reporting and eligibility for honors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous standards of reporting vs retrospective judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Many award-winning reports would be seen differently in later years; reassessing past awards through present-day norms can be fraught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should balance historical context and the standards of the time against present understandings; caution is advised when retroactively applying modern norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational credibility context
rubrics_metrics.description: A news organization's recent scandals or credibility problems can affect its willingness or ability to re-evaluate past awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times' own credibility crises (e.g., Judith Miller, Jayson Blair) influenced its approach to re-assessing Duranty; institutional context can color both internal and external calls for revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural authority for rescinding awards
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision to rescind a Pulitzer rests with the Pulitzer Prize board, which is overseen by Columbia University; a news organization can request action but does not unilaterally revoke Pulitzer honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding who has jurisdiction and the formal procedures is part of evaluating and acting on concerns about awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary withdrawal or institutional requests for correction
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations can ask prize boards to rescind honors or can return awards themselves (e.g., NYT asked board to take back Caliphate honors and returned a Peabody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations have mechanisms to correct the record proactively, including requesting revocation from awarding bodies or returning prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth, corroboration, and breadth of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern standards favor broader reporting teams and multiple correspondents rather than a single correspondent defining a major story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joseph Kahn notes the Times now has many reporters on major stories (e.g., 40 journalists in Ukraine), suggesting that corroboration, on-the-ground breadth, and multiple sources are current quality criteria for international reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the honored work (interpretive reporting vs factual accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pulitzer board cited Duranty's "dispassionate interpretive reporting" when awarding the prize, highlighting interpretive work as a category distinct from straightforward factual reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards may be given for interpretive or analytical reporting as well as for straightforward fact-reporting; evaluating such work should consider the standards appropriate to its genre (analysis, context-setting, sourcing), not only binary factual correctness.
